I always just trimmed the sides in. Like: https://imgur.com/a/gVGZoCs

The solid lines are the original shirt, the dotted lines are where I take them in--basically just creating a new seam, and then you cut away the old one/excess fabric (you know you sew the new seam with the shirt inside out, I assume, but I'm mentioning it just in case, because I know when I very first started sewing I didn't know that). It's easiest to lay the shirt flat, inside out, and measure its width at various points, then subtract the new width that you want from that number. Divide that amount in half, and you'll know how much to take in from each side. Measure and do the math several times, because if your measurements are off by a cm or so it won't be a big deal but more than that and the shirt will "feel" crooked even if it doesn't look it, and nobody wants that. :-)

So measure measure measure, pin carefully--use as many pins as you want--and carefully try it on (keep in mind that the extra fabric inside will make it seem bulkier on the sides than it will be when it's done). If you like, you can baste a new seam rather than pinning--basting is basically sewing the new seam with big long stitches; they won't hold it permanently or anything and they won't look nice, but you'll be able to try it on without worrying about getting pins stuck in your sides, and you won't have the bulk and stiffness of pins so you'll get a better idea how the finished product will look. If you like the basting, do a nice single line of stitches--I usually do a tight backstitch here--on the baste line (you can remove the basting at that point) and try it on again. If that's right, trim the excess fabric out and do a second line of stitches; you can do another line of backstitches right by the cut edge, or a whipstitch (overcast stitch) which sews the raw edges together. I usually do the latter, but either is fine. Just keep those stitches small and steady--too-tight stitches will create unsightly bulges/gaps/crooked spaces in the shirt's seam. If your hand-sewing is rusty, try doing this on an old shirt you don't wear or wouldn't mind making a little crookedy or whatever first. :-)

Sleeves are a little trickier, and I generally leave them alone unless I have no choice, but it can be done--you just want to be really careful. It might even be worth taking in the sides of the shirt up "into" the sleeve--that is to say, past the point where the bottom of the sleeve meets the body of the shirt, up to the point where you want the bottom of the sleeve to start--and then sew a new "bottom" seam of the sleeve from there.

Our neighbors/close friends inherited a small-but-decent chunk of money, and they were thinking now might be the time to upgrade to a bigger house, since they now have a son and a daughter, so the kids sharing a bedroom won't be feasible in a few years. The problem is, the contract they signed says that if they decide to take the house off the market before the end of the listing term, they have to pay the broker $995.00. Which all of us think is ridiculous. Really, a thousand dollars if you decide not to sell? To "cover hard costs incurred by [Realtor]?" Fuck you. Those "hard costs" are the cost of doing business. If my agent doesn't sell a client's mss, the client isn't on the hook for costs incurred; if a publisher puts out a book that flops, the author isn't on the hook for publishing costs. I'm reading the contract right now to see if I can spot any loopholes or anything (IANAL, and while I know a lot about publishing contracts & used to help other writers with theirs, this obviously isn't a publishing contract and I'm looking at it--at their request--more as a "Let's all look at it and put our heads together" kind of thing, not as a "I'm an expert at contracts" kind of thing. I think I've spotted one possible way they can get out of it already, but again, I'm no expert. Yo bud, the point of those clauses (often called breakup or termination fees) is that you have a set term for the realtor to sell the house in -- and pulling out early incurs a penalty. TONS of contracts have clauses like this, and you hear about it all the time especially in corporate M&A. They're boilerplate legal work and there is no way to "get out" of it unless, say, the realtor is in breach.

That being said, you can always try to drop it, refuse to pay, and tell the realtor to take it to small claims (but your friend will likely lose).

Well, yeah, we understand the point of the clause/its purpose, and that it's apparently a common clause these days (it wasn't when I last sold a house!). And if it comes down to it they'll just wait out the rest of the term--that just seems like it would be wasting more of the realtor's time and money, which they think is ridiculous and makes them feel bad. They don't like the idea of the realtor actually doing more work for them with no hope of payment, despite their feeling that the realtors have been rather underhanded in general (see next para).

The reason they even signed that contract and put the house on the market to begin with (when they originally called the realtor just for a consultation, basically) was because the realtor told them they'd be able to get a much larger asking price than they thought, and quickly. The realtor mentioned being aware of this problem before they signed--but let them sign anyway, which we all find rather sleazy, and which means the house is ultimately worth even less again/they'd get even less for it, but the realtor's commission would be the same (as in, the realtor gets commission on the full asking price but our neighbors would have to give up a chunk of their profit to fix the problem for the buyer--as I'm sure you know, I don't mean to imply you don't, I'm just kind of explaining for anyone else reading this). So again, the feeling is that the realtor kind of got them to sign under false pretenses/misled them a bit.

This is where we wonder if it's possible that the realtor is in breach in some way. I realize it sounds rather rich to say we're all pretty honest and honorable people, given that the subject here is trying to get out of a contract they signed, but they feel like it was/is pretty dishonest for a realtor to agree to sell a house with foundation issues without disclosing those issues even to them, much less to a buyer, and that makes them not want to work with these people--and aside from everything else, they wouldn't feel right about selling to others without disclosing or fixing the problem, which is the biggest reason why they no longer want to sell and have decided to renovate instead (I didn't want to go on and on into all of the details in my OP). They figure if they have to spend their nest egg fixing problems with the house anyway, they might as well convert the garage into a bedroom as well so that when they are ready to actually sell in five years or so, not only will the house be in a condition they feel comfortable passing on but the extra bedroom will make it more comparable to other houses in the area and more valuable/attractive. (These are 3/2 houses, but a prior owner converted their 3rd bed into a dining room, so it's only a 2/2. That bedroom can't be converted back, because the porch was extended and turned into a den, and the window of that bedroom was turned into a pass-through that opens to that den--so there is no egress for that room, basically, which means it's illegal to make it a bedroom.)

Anyway, thanks for reading, and for your thoughts--I do really appreciate it!

So based on these details: if the realtor promised to sell above their expected asking price (even verbally), simply leave it up for the duration and tell him you're only interested in selling for the elevated price. The term lapses, and your friend is out.

If the realtor tries to sell for a shit price, refuse, let the term lapse, and you're out. If he claims refusing the lower price means you violated the agreement to sell (which can vary depending on how it is worded), THEN tell him to fuck off and take it to court. With this fact pattern, there's a much lower chance for him to succeed -- meaning he's less likely to risks to costs of litigation for just $1000.

Aside: if the realtor was aware of this problem and still told your friends to sign the contract, that is textbook fraud in the inducement and the contract is invalid entirely. That is something I'd report to whatever your state's licensing board is to investigate.

Ethics disclaimer: None of this is intended as actual legal advice. For that, consult a local lawyer.
